h.strategy: Most obvious hypotheses follow a local story: an option matters more when its substitute is missing. These are usually rated likely and often fail. Instead, base hypotheses on robust statistical regularities. (1) Headroom: helpful edits help less in parents that are already strong, for example parents that already contain the strongest option elsewhere. (2) Harmful edits hurt more in strong parents and look harmless in weak parents, because of floor effects. (3) Saturation: adding a second copy of a strong option gives smaller gains than adding the first. (4) Removing an option costs less when the parent has several similar options. Choose conditions that many parents satisfy, so the effect is detectable. Cover several edited fields and both directions. In each 'why', state the obvious prediction and the reason the opposite should hold.

hyps.why: Obvious: removing edge 4 hurts equally anywhere; but a skip on edge 3 supplies a gradient and feature path to the output, so losing edge 4 costs less.
Obvious: cutting the first edge is damaging everywhere; but a strong direct 0->3 conv gives a bypass that makes the removal comparatively cheap.
Obvious: removing an inner edge costs the same everywhere; but a strong conv on edge 1 into node 2 already supplies similar information, so the removal costs less.
Obvious: a strong direct edge compensates for a weak edge 1; but a harmful edit shows more in a high-accuracy parent, while weak parents sit near the floor and hide the damage.
Obvious: losing a strong input is costly; but with a similar strong edge 4 into node 3 the removal is largely redundant, so the cost is smaller (similar-option redundancy).
Obvious: skips help the output node wherever added; but a second skip into node 3 duplicates the first one's path, giving diminishing returns.
Obvious: skip on the last edge improves gradient flow regardless; but with a skip already on edge 3 the gradient path exists, so the marginal benefit is small.
Obvious: a conv on the inner edge adds depth; but when the final edge already has a 3x3 conv the architecture is near its ceiling and extra inner capacity adds little.
Obvious: removing edge 3 hurts less when a strong alternate path exists; but strong parents sit high above the floor, so any removal drops more than in weak parents that are already near the floor.
Obvious: strengthening the first-layer edge helps regardless; but with a 3x3 conv on the other input edge the early features are already strong, so the marginal gain is smaller.
